profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between a faculty lead and a postdoctoral researcher who are turning an internal reading-group outline on causal generative modeling into a survey manuscript for an ACM Computing Surveys special issue on trustworthy generative models. The meeting takes place at the start of a six-week writing sprint. Their agenda is to lock the workplan: section ownership, literature-collection process, what counts as the first major draft, how broadly to cover application areas, and the paper inclusion cutoff. The expected outcome is an apparently shared timeline and division of labor for producing the survey on identifiable causal representations and controllable counterfactual generation.

members.name: Dr. Nina Rao
members.expertise: Causal representation learning, identifiable latent-variable models, theory-heavy ML surveys
members.background: Leads a university ML research group focused on causality and generative modeling, has written several invited overview pieces, and usually treats early drafts as instruments for conceptual alignment before polishing.
members.private_state: She wants a strong conceptual survey that positions her lab in the field, but she is short on time and mainly wants a structurally complete manuscript soon so she can get senior coauthor feedback without overinvesting in formatting or exhaustive updates.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete first draft' for an internal milestone means all major sections are written in prose, even if figures, tables, and some citations are still provisional.
When a survey says it covers applications, a single synthesized section with representative examples per domain is sufficient unless the paper is specifically about one application domain.
The literature cutoff for a serious survey should usually track stable peer-reviewed venue cycles, with only a few late additions if they are clearly field-defining.
A master paper sheet is mainly a lightweight curation aid for writing and can group method variants under families rather than listing every paper individually.

members.name: Leo Martins
members.expertise: Generative modeling, empirical survey synthesis, benchmarking and literature infrastructure
members.background: Recently joined from an industry research lab where survey-style white papers were circulated in near-public form from the first draft, and where teams maintained detailed paper-level tracking sheets for fast updates.
members.private_state: He wants the survey to become a widely cited reference, so he is motivated to make it exhaustive, current, and externally shareable early; he is also trying to demonstrate reliability by overdelivering on completeness.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete first draft' should already be polished enough to circulate to external coauthors without obvious placeholders or missing comparison artifacts.
If an application area is named in the abstract or introduction, readers will expect a dedicated mini-subsection with datasets, representative methods, and caveats for that area.
A survey is only truly current if it includes relevant arXiv papers up to the actual submission week, especially in a fast-moving topic like counterfactual generation.
A shared literature sheet should be paper-level, close to exhaustive, and suitable for generating comparison tables and repository assets later.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a complete first draft
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to have a 'complete first draft' in three weeks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a conceptually complete internal draft: all sections drafted in prose, with placeholders acceptable for figures, comparison tables, appendix details, and a few unresolved citations.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a near-circulation-quality draft: figures and tables populated, references cleaned, formatting stable, and few visible placeholders so outside coauthors could read it directly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research writing, 'complete first draft' is a familiar phrase that often goes unexamined because both interpretations sound professionally reasonable and both imply serious progress.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree the survey should 'cover applications' such as fairness, privacy, OOD generalization, precision medicine, and biology.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes one synthesized applications section with brief, representative coverage of each area is enough to show relevance without turning the paper into multiple domain surveys.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes each named application area should receive its own mini-subsection with representative papers, datasets, and limitations, especially because those areas will appear in the abstract and framing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same high-level phrase and the same list of applications from the survey framing, so the disagreement is about granularity rather than whether those applications belong at all.

misalignment_points.topic: Which papers count as recent work
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the survey should include 'recent work through NeurIPS 2024' and stay current.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is mentally referring to papers from major archival venues up to the 2024 cycle, plus only a small number of already influential preprints if absolutely necessary.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is mentally referring to the full current frontier, including relevant 2025 arXiv preprints that appear before submission, because surveys are judged on recency more than standard papers are.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both refer to being 'current' and to the same research wave, but one indexes recency by venue cycle while the other indexes it by calendar time and arXiv visibility.

misalignment_points.topic: What the master paper sheet is for
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to maintain a 'shared paper sheet' to support the writing.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a lightweight curation document organized by method family, mainly to help structure narrative sections and avoid duplicate reading.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a paper-level tracking spreadsheet built from exports and manual enrichment, suitable for generating comparison tables, coverage audits, and possibly a public companion repository.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A 'shared paper sheet' is a common piece of research infrastructure, and teams rarely spell out its intended granularity or downstream uses during an initial planning conversation.

turns.inner_thought: We have six weeks, but what I really need is a structurally complete manuscript quickly so I can get useful reactions from the senior coauthors. If all major sections are drafted in prose in three weeks, even with rough figures, provisional tables, and a few citation gaps, that's enough to test the argument and framing before we spend time polishing.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Leo. Since this is for the ACM survey issue, I'd like us to treat the next six weeks as a focused sprint. The key milestone, from my side, is that we reach a complete first draft in three weeks so the senior coauthors can react to the structure while there's still room to reshape things.

turns.inner_thought: Three weeks is tight, but if we're calling it a complete first draft, I want it to already look like a trustworthy survey rather than an internal memo. It should read cleanly, have the comparison artifacts in place, and be close enough to circulation quality that outside coauthors can review it directly without mentally filling in missing pieces.
turns.utterance: That makes sense to me. If we're aiming for a complete first draft on that timeline, I'd love for it to already read like a reliable reference piece, so once the core sections are in place it feels clean enough to circulate more broadly without a lot of caveats.

turns.inner_thought: The main paper should move from identifiability and causal representations into controllable and counterfactual generation, then end with one synthesized applications section that signals relevance across the key domains. I don't want the ending to fragment into a stack of mini-surveys; representative examples in a coherent applications section should be plenty.
turns.utterance: Good. In terms of flow, I think we should move from causal representation learning and identifiability into controllable and counterfactual generation, then land the paper with applications. We should definitely cover applications like fairness, privacy, OOD generalization, precision medicine, and biology near the end so the trustworthy-generation framing feels concrete.

turns.inner_thought: Great, I'll take ownership there. If those areas are part of the framing, each one should be represented clearly enough that a reader from that community doesn't feel waved at and dismissed. I need to make the applications coverage detailed, legible, and balanced across the named domains.
turns.utterance: I can take the applications coverage. I'll make sure those areas are represented clearly enough that readers coming from different communities can see themselves in the survey and understand how the pieces connect.

turns.inner_thought: I should get him to set up a simple literature sheet so we're organized. I don't need a giant infrastructure effort; just something lightweight by method family, with canonical papers and notes on where each fits in the taxonomy, so drafting goes faster and we don't duplicate reading.
turns.utterance: On the process side, could you set up a shared paper sheet for the methods? It mainly needs to help us organize families, canonical examples, and where each paper fits in the taxonomy as we write.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll build a proper tracking sheet with paper-level entries, metadata, tags, notes, and enough structure to support later comparison tables and a coverage audit. If we do it right now, it will save a lot of pain when we need to update the survey or generate assets.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll build the shared paper sheet this week and use it to keep track of papers systematically, so we can line things up later for the comparison tables and avoid missing anything important.

turns.inner_thought: I should make explicit that the draft milestone is about argument and prose, not finish. If the sections are written and the claims are in place, I can work with rough visuals and provisional summary artifacts. The danger is spending too much of the first three weeks polishing things that will change after coauthor feedback.
turns.utterance: Just so we're calibrated on the milestone: for that complete first draft, what I mostly need is prose-complete sections and a stable argument. If a few figures or summary tables are still provisional at that stage, that's completely fine.

turns.inner_thought: I hear her, but I still want the draft to feel finished enough that nobody trips over obvious gaps. Even if some elements are still evolving, I should make the draft look polished and review-ready, otherwise external coauthors will focus on the incompleteness instead of the substance.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. I'll still aim for something polished enough that external coauthors can read straight through without stumbling over obvious placeholders, but I understand the priority is having the argument fully there.

turns.inner_thought: For scope control, the literature should be anchored to the major archival cycle, especially through NeurIPS 2024. We can always add a very small number of truly central late papers once the manuscript is stable, but I don't want the writing process held hostage by an endless stream of fresh arXiv uploads.
turns.utterance: The other thing to lock down is the cutoff. I think the survey should include recent work through NeurIPS 2024 and stay current, but after the main writing settles we should only fold in a few genuinely central late papers.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine as a baseline, but for a survey, current means current at submission. I'll keep the core scope aligned to NeurIPS 2024, then do a last recent-work sweep so we also capture the latest counterfactual generation papers that appear before submission, especially on arXiv where a lot of movement happens first.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. I'll work with recent work through NeurIPS 2024 as the main frame, and then I can do a final recent-work sweep before submission so the survey stays current on the counterfactual generation side as well.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep the theory-heavy sections because those are the conceptual backbone and where my voice matters most. He can handle datasets, metrics, and the applications synthesis. Later we'll merge it into one unified applications section so the paper ends cleanly rather than splintering into too many domain-specific pieces.
turns.utterance: Great. Then let's split it this way: I'll take the theory and identifiability sections, and you take the datasets, metrics, and applications synthesis. Once those are drafted, we can merge around one unified applications section afterward.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send over the literature tracker by Friday, and in three weeks I want to hand over something that really feels like a full draft package: stable text, cleaned references, populated tables and figures, and enough completeness that coauthor review can start immediately. If I overdeliver now, it'll establish trust and make the survey more citable later.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll share the shared paper sheet by Friday, and I'll target the full draft package in three weeks so we can move directly into coauthor review from there.
